start: ^Tomasz: You're the one giving me a headache this week. Good. I asked for it.
^Tomasz: Tomasz. I run security here, me and half a person's budget.
^Tomasz: Two jobs for you. Triage that inbox at the workstation, then flip the board and pick the fixes.

b: ^Tomasz: Both done. Sit down, let's close this out.
^Tomasz: Come back when you've finished the exercise. Both halves.

hub: ^Why does the service desk keep coming up?

c-3: ^Tomasz: Take your time. I'm not going anywhere.

own_mail: ^Tomasz: Two of those are yours. The ones you sent Melanie and Sofia, landing in my queue.
^Tomasz: Mark them like any other. The header panel shows exactly why they were catchable.
dev_finding: ^Tomasz: Dev's good at his job. The policy let him hand that out, so the policy's the problem.
^Tomasz: We're writing Dev a script, not a warning. Call back on a number we hold.
debrief: ^Tomasz: Here's what it showed. An open inbox trusts anyone, a From line is just a label, and a padlock proves nothing.

b: ^Tomasz: You landed Melanie first try. That's how good a borrowed name is — it beats careful people every time.
^Tomasz: And Dev reported you. Credit to him — but a call-back rule would have caught it without him noticing a thing.
^Tomasz: Dev handed you the portal and the date, no fuss. A call-back to a number on file stops every line of that.
^Tomasz: You had to lean on Dev to get the portal and the date, but he still gave them up. A call-back to a number on file stops every line of that.

debrief: ^Tomasz: So we route the open inbox through a gateway, strip document metadata, and give the desk that call-back script.
^Tomasz: And the report. No names. Gareth reads it, nobody feels hunted, people keep telling us when they slip.
^Tomasz: That last part is the whole job. Blame them once and they stop reporting. Thanks for playing it straight.
